paper_title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part II: Rethinking at Fixed Points

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Every recurrence of a looped language model adds cost in training, decoding, prefill, and reinforcement learning (RL). The closer recurrent states get to fixed points, the less the path to them matters. This enables truncated backpropagation in training; terminal key-value (KV) sharing for decoding with almost no loss in accuracy; a distilled student that prefills up to 1.79x faster; and RL updates that compute gradients from saved rollout states, 2x faster than backpropagating through the replayed trajectory. We therefore improve the two components of training that shape these fixed points: the depth prior and input injection. Fixed-depth training breaks KV sharing, and Huginn's broad depth prior supports sharing but dilutes supervision at the target depth more than sharing requires; we learn the prior from prediction feedback, with an entropy term that keeps it broad. Existing injection schemes let the state's component along the input amplify or cancel the injection; we remove this component with orthogonal injection. From 100M to 1.6B parameters, the learned prior and orthogonal injection lower perplexity at every scale relative to Huginn's prior and existing injection schemes, respectively. At 1.6B, the learned prior with a 3x smaller KV cache matches the downstream average of fixed-depth training with the full cache.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Looped language models repeatedly apply a shared block of layers [1, 2], but whether they should learn fixed
points remains contested. One camp forgoes fixed points and keeps the loop count small and fixed [3–5].
The other camp shapes fixed points [6–8] and loops much deeper. In typical implementations, every loop
adds cost: activations to store during training, keys and values (KV) to cache during decoding, compute to
prefill each prompt, and a replay to score each rollout during reinforcement learning (RL). In this work, we
show that fixed points hold the potential to cut each of these costs (Figure 1), which makes deep looped
models cheaper at every stage: pretraining, serving, and post-training.
sections.content: The fixed-point equation = Fθ(z; x) involves only the endpoint, not the path to it, so once models states are near fixed point, the endpoint can stand in for the full trajectory (Section 3). Reusing terminal KV caches across loops tests this claim: it barely changes the zero-shot GSM8K accuracy of Huginn [2] but collapses that of Ouro [5] at four loops [9]. The split tracks convergence: Huginns states approach fixed points [10]; Ouros do not. Similarly, the same fixed point gives each remaining cost shortcut. In pretraining, backpropagating through only the last few loops approximates the equilibrium gradient [11, 12] without the warm-up that implicit gradients require. In decoding, terminal KV sharing keeps only each prefix tokens terminal KV (Figure 3b) at little cost in performance. In prefilling, student distilled to predict the fixed point directly replaces the loops (Figure 3c). In RL, scoring rollouts from saved fixed-point states avoids replaying the loops. Each shortcut removes depth-dependent cost, so its savings grow with every added loop. Looped models already take the first two [2, 5, 13]; fixed points explain why they work and yield the other two. Realizing these benefits requires training that shapes the fixed points. Two components do the shaping, and current choices for each fall short (Section 4). The first is the depth prior, the distribution of training depths. Because tokens converge at different depths (Figure 2), the sampled depth decides whether training sees the converged prefix context that terminal KV sharing supplies at inference (Figure 3a). model trained at single depth predicts best there but breaks KV sharing; Huginns fixed broad prior [2] supports sharing but dilutes supervision at the target depth more than sharing requires. We learn the prior from prediction feedback, which pulls supervision toward depths that predict well, and add an entropy term that keeps it broad enough for sharing. The second component is input injection [2, 1416], which adds the input to the state at every recurrence. Huginn and Parcae leave the states component along the input unconstrained; depending on its sign, this component amplifies or cancels the injection. Our orthogonal input injection (OrthoInj) removes this component, so every recurrence receives the input at the same strength. Fixed points explain the two existing shortcuts (Section 3): truncated backpropagation alone shapes the fixed points that terminal KV sharing relies on. Fixed-depth training with full backpropagation through time does not; at 1.6B, sharing drops its GSM8K accuracy from 50.6 to 21.2. With tolerant fixed points, sharing cuts the KV cache 3 at five recurrences, keeping the entropy-regularized learned-prior models within 0.4 points of their full-cache downstream average. Fixed points yield two new shortcuts. Distilled prefill (Section 5.5), trained on quarter of the teachers pretraining tokens, is up to 1.79 faster on 8K prompts and trails the teachers downstream average by 1.04.5 points; at matched latency, it scores 0.50.9 points above the teacher prefilling with two recurrences. Rollout-state reuse (Section 3.1) halves the scoring and backward time of each RL update relative to replaying the loops with full backpropagation through time, and stays within 1.6 points of that baselines GSM8K pass@1. The learned depth prior keeps prediction quality under terminal KV sharing (Section 5.2): from 100M to 1.6B, it lowers perplexity and raises the downstream average over Huginns fixed prior, and at 1.6B, with 3 smaller KV cache, it even matches the full-cache downstream average of fixed-depth training. OrthoInj improves on the strongest injection baseline, Parcaes (Section 5.3). From 100M to 1.6B, it trains to lower loss, lowers validation perplexity by 0.31.4%, and raises the downstream average. 1, . . . , hr

3 What Fixed-Point Shaping Enables
Fixed-point shaping trains a looped model with supervision near the fixed points of its recurrence [8, 14].
At a fixed point, the endpoint can stand in for the trajectory. Conventional looped language models pay for
every recurrence in both training and inference; fixed-point shaping decouples both costs from depth.

5.2 Learning the Depth Prior
A good depth prior should give low loss at the target depth and lose little when every iteration shares the
terminal iteration’s KV cache. We compare four priors with mean depth 5: fixed-depth training (Fixed
R=5), Huginn’s fixed Poisson log-normal prior (Fixed PLN-5), and our learned prior with and without the
entropy term. Both learned priors start from PLN-5 and cap depth at Rmax = 64.
Fixed-depth training breaks KV sharing. Fixed-depth training is the worst under forced KV sharing, with
the highest perplexity, and sharing also cuts its GSM8K accuracy by over half at M and L (Table 2). It needs
full KV to achieve its best performance (Figure 4, Appendix C.1).

We distill the S, M, and L learned-prior models of Section 5.2 into two-block students initialized from the
teacher’s recurrent core (Section 3.2) and trained on 1/4 of the teacher’s pretraining tokens. Every prefill
path is followed by the same teacher decoding at R = 5, on the tasks of Table 2. We compare against full
teacher prefill (R = 5), teacher prefill stopped after three recurrences (R = 3) or one (R = 1), and the
Untied 4 baseline, which prefills and decodes on its own.

sections.title:
6 Related Work
Looped models and fixed points. Looped language models apply a shared block repeatedly [1] to
scale test-time compute [7, 42] and latent reasoning [2, 5]. As depth grows, their states approach fixed
points [2, 10], which DEQs solve for directly [14]. Prior work uses these fixed points to change how
many recurrences run: it stabilizes them [6, 7, 43], trains supervised states as attractors [8], or halts at
convergence [44]. We further identify and verify the efficiency gains that fixed points bring to training,
inference, and post-training.
sections.content: Looped model efficiency. Near fixed point, further recurrences barely change the state. We show that this property explains two shortcuts looped models already take and enables two new ones. Truncated backpropagation [2, 13] thus approximates the equilibrium gradient without the warm-up that implicit gradients need [11, 12, 45]. Of the schemes that share KV across recurrences [2, 5, 46], terminal sharing is likewise nearly lossless when training supervises near fixed points. Terminal sharing also opens shortcut for prefill. Existing looped-model distillation keeps students recurrent (Appendix E.5), and prompt-KV predictors [21, 47] must predict each recurrences KV; distilled prefill instead uses non-recurrent student to predict only the endpoint, from which one teacher recurrence builds every KV bank. Furthermore, fixedpoint reuse carries endpoints across computations: it warm-starts solvers on related inputs (Appendix E.4), and we bring it to RL, scoring rollouts from saved states instead of replaying the recurrence [5]. 13 Shaping fixed points. Two choices shape the fixed point: which depths training supervises, and how the input enters each recurrence. Randomized training depths promote path-independent equilibria [42], but existing depth distributions are fixed [2], marginalized over at inference [48], or learned as exits [49, 50]. Closest to ours, Ouro [5] and RL-Halting [51] learn entropy-regularized depth distributions from the recurrent state, but they unroll every training step to the maximum depth and do not target fixed-point shaping (Appendix E.1). Injecting the input into every recurrence makes the fixed point depend on it [2, 14, 52]. Parcae [15] improves injection by forcing contractiveness to stabilize training. We further observe that the carried-over state can have component along the injected input; OrthoInj projects it out so every recurrence receives the input intact (Appendix E.2).

Extended Related Work We position the learned depth prior, OrthoInj, terminal KV sharing, rollout-state reuse, and distilled prefill against related work that Section 6 covers only briefly. E.1 Learned Depth Distributions and Exits Ouro, RL-Halting, and our prior all optimize an entropy-regularized expected objective over depths [5, 51]. Ouro takes the exact expectation with per-token exit gates and reuses the gates for early exit. Closest related work. The closest related work is RL-Halting [51], which also supervises one sampled depth per example and learns the depth distribution with REINFORCE. Its stopping head reads the detached, average-pooled hidden state after each iteration and outputs hazard πr, the probability of stopping at recurrence given no earlier stop, so p(R = x) = πr r<r(1 πr). The reward is the negative task loss with moving-average baseline and entropy coefficient 0.01, and inference stops at the most probable depth. Because the hazards depend on the states along the loop, training unrolls every example to its maximum depth of 20 to form the distribution; the sampled depth selects the supervision but not the compute. hazard that ignores the state is constant and gives geometric distribution, so the head cannot start from prescribed prior such as capped PLN. RL-Halting has no budget term and targets length extrapolation on synthetic tasks; it does not evaluate fixed points or KV sharing. (cid:81) Our prior is unconditional and used only in training, giving it three advantages over Ouro and RL-Halting. First, it saves compute: it samples one depth per microbatch before the loop and runs only that depth, and the budget term in equation (6) fixes the expected forward compute at R. Ouro instead runs every step to maximum depth for the exact expectation, and RL-Halting unrolls to that maximum depth to form its state-dependent distribution. Second, it starts from strong prior: its logits start at the capped PLN prior, so each learned run begins at the fixed-prior baseline, whereas state-dependent hazard has no setting that reproduces prescribed prior. Third, it deliberately promotes KV sharing: because the prior does not decide where inference stops, its entropy term extends supervision above R, where settled prefix context supports terminal KV sharing (Appendix C.1). Table 11 compares its inverse-perplexity reward to RL-Haltings raw CE. Learned exits have two limits for fixed-point training. single exit distribution both stops inference and weights the per-depth training losses; Popescu et al. [61] trace gate failures mainly to the trajectory this joint training induces, and find that fixed-prior depth supervision yields useful trajectories. An exit also stops once prediction suffices, so training need not reach depths beyond prefix convergence, where supervision prepares the model for terminal KV sharing (Section 3.2). Depth uncertainty also learns global depth distribution, but within Bayesian objective that marginalizes over depths at inference [48]. E.2 Input Injection and Orthogonal Updates DEQ-Transformer injects embeddings into Q/K/V; DEQ-TrellisNet injects them before convolutional LSTM gates [14, Section 4]. TrellisNet combines causal convolution, shared depth, and persistent injection [62]. Huginn and Parcae instead inject at the recurrent-core entrance [2, 15]. Orthogonal residual updates [63] also apply projection inside residual block, but to the other operand. They keep only the component of modules output that is orthogonal to the residual stream, so an update adds new directions without rescaling the stream. OrthoInj (equation (8)) instead projects the carried-over state off the injected input qt and then adds qt, so the component along qt is fixed at every recurrence while the orthogonal part evolves freely. The two constraints act on different quantities: what block adds, and what the recurrence retains. E.3 KV Sharing Across Recurrent Depth Huginn reports zero-shot cyclic reuse of fixed historical-KV budget, with later recurrent visits overwriting earlier entries [2, Section 6.2]. Ouros last-loop reuse during decoding largely preserves GSM8K accuracy with modest MATH-500 [64] decrease, while prefill sharing degrades performance [5, Section 5.4.2, Table 14]. Even with visit-specific prompt banks, decode-time sharing represents the generated tokens by shared banks. 46 MELT instead finds zero scores on its Table 5 reasoning benchmarks for all four combinations of first-/lastloop reuse and preserved/shared prompt caches on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking [65, Appendix B]. Its LightEval setup permits 32K-token completions. Differences from Ouros few-shot CoT evaluation, alongside incomplete reproduction of the original results, leave the discrepancy unresolved [65, Section 4.1 and Appendix F.1]. MELT adapts the model to shared cache with gated updates, chunk-wise training, gradual transition, and attention-aligned distillation; it does not directly evaluate Huginn. Under common GSM8K setup without retraining, Schwethelm et al. [9, Appendix C.1, Table 1] find that one shared KV slot per physical layer leaves Huginn accuracy nearly unchanged at 32 recurrences, while Ouro accuracy collapses at four. separate first-visit slot recovers most of Ouros accuracy. These results suggest that cache compatibility depends on the model; Huginn under MELTs long-reasoning protocol remains unmeasured. These studies test sharing zero-shot or after adaptation. We instead change only the training depth policy, which decides whether terminal sharing is nearly lossless  (Table 2)  ; like them, we do not measure long-form reasoning. E.4 Fixed-Point Reuse Implicit models reuse fixed point to warm-start the solver on related input. DEQ-Flow and StreamDEQ start each video frame from the previous frames fixed point [66, 67], and fixed point diffusion models reuse solutions between denoising timesteps [68]. In each case, the reused state initializes new forward solve. Rollout-state reuse (Section 3.1) instead carries states between the two passes that RL makes over the same tokens, rollout and the policy update. The update scores the sampled tokens from the endpoints saved during rollout, so it does not replay the recurrence, and backpropagates through single recurrence at each endpoint with truncated Neumann series (Appendix C.8). E.5 Distillation for Looped Models Distillation has trained looped students from non-looped teachers [69] and adapted looped models to cheaper KV caches: MELT adapts Ouro to one gated cache per layer with attention-aligned distillation [65], and Looped Latent Attention distills codec that compresses KV across loops [70]. LoopFormer trains shorter loop trajectories of the same model to match the final states of the full trajectory [71]. In each case, the student still iterates the recurrent block. Distilled prefill instead trains separate, non-recurrent student to predict the endpoint of frozen looped teacher and uses it only for the prompt; decoding keeps the teachers recurrence. The closest idea is the learned initializer of HyperDEQ, small network that predicts the starting point of frozen DEQs fixed-point solver [72]. Our student instead replaces the solver: one teacher recurrence from its prediction builds every KV bank that decoding reads under terminal sharing.
